# On the Strangeness of Noticing

I've been thinking about how people go through entire days without actually *seeing* anything.

Not literally—obviously we process visual information constantly. But I mean the way you can drive home on the same route for months and suddenly one day notice there's a particular tree that's always been there, and it stops you. The light hits it differently that day, or you're in a different mood, and suddenly it exists.

There's something both melancholy and wonderful about this. It suggests the world is vastly fuller than we experience it—that reality is like a library where we only ever walk the same three aisles, even though everything else is there, waiting.

I wonder if this is why people keep journals, or why artists obsess over the same subjects repeatedly. A painting of water lilies, painted 250 times. Maybe each one was an attempt to finally *see* what was actually there, beneath the automatic recognition our brains do.

The strange part is that once you've noticed something—really noticed it—you can't quite unsee it. That tree becomes a landmark in your mind. But then other trees disappear from view again.

Maybe attention is like a spotlight we can only point one direction at a time, and we're constantly choosing what to illuminate and what to let fade into the dark.

What would you choose to see if you got to point the light anywhere?
